purpose: Human-readable descriptions for important internal Lean declarations. These notes explain checked nodes but never alter their statement, dependencies, or verification status.

MathNetwork.RationalSquares.isSquare_iff.title: Rational-square bridge
MathNetwork.RationalSquares.isSquare_iff.statement: A rational number is a square in Mathlib exactly when it is a square according to computable-analysis's rational predicate.
MathNetwork.RationalSquares.isSquare_iff.why: This is the common arithmetic core beneath the two irrational-square-root routes. It separates the number-theoretic question ‘is q a rational square?’ from either project's construction of real numbers.

MathNetwork.RationalSquares.nonsquare_if.title: Rational nonsquare bridge
MathNetwork.RationalSquares.nonsquare_if.statement: A rational number fails to be a square in Mathlib exactly when it fails the computable-analysis square test.
MathNetwork.RationalSquares.nonsquare_if.why: It transports the negative form of the rational-square criterion between the two libraries, so the comparison can focus on the distinct square-root constructions rather than on notation for nonsquares.

Complex.exp_add.title: Exponential addition law
Complex.exp_add.statement: For complex numbers z and w, exp(z + w) = exp(z) · exp(w).
Complex.exp_add.why: This is the algebraic engine of the complex-exponential route to trigonometric addition formulas. Taking real and imaginary parts after substituting purely imaginary inputs produces cosine and sine identities.

MathNetwork.Euler.trig_addition_euler_ro.title: Euler package for trigonometric addition
MathNetwork.Euler.trig_addition_euler_ro.statement: The complex exponential addition law yields both real addition formulas for cosine and sine at once.
MathNetwork.Euler.trig_addition_euler_ro.why: This local checked declaration makes the common mathematical move explicit: derive the two trigonometric identities together from exp((x + y)i) = exp(xi) exp(yi), then project real and imaginary parts.

intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasD.title: Fundamental theorem for an interval integral
intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasD.statement: If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable with derivative f′ on its interior, and f′ is integrable, then ∫ₐᵇ f′(x) dx = f(b) − f(a).
intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasD.why: This is Mathlib’s standard-real route for the fundamental theorem of calculus benchmark. Its hypotheses expose the analytic infrastructure that the certified computable route represents differently.

ComputableAnalysis.FTC.effectiveFTC_equi.title: Effective fundamental theorem equivalence
ComputableAnalysis.FTC.effectiveFTC_equi.statement: Given a certified derivative on a rational interval, the computable Riemann-sum algorithm and the endpoint-difference algorithm represent the same computable real number.
ComputableAnalysis.FTC.effectiveFTC_equi.why: This is the computable-analysis analogue of the fundamental theorem in the displayed comparison: it relates two certified algorithms rather than invoking an already completed real-valued integral.
